as_told.title: Air Force closes Project Blue Book

tellings.quote: Careful consideration of the record as it is available to us leads us to conclude that further extensive study of UFOs probably cannot be justified in the expectation that science will be advanced thereby.

It is our impression that the defense function could be performed within the framework established for intelligence and surveillance operations without the continuance of a special unit such as Project Blue Book, but this is a question for defense specialists rather than research scientists.
On December 17, 1969, the Secretary of the Air Force announced the termination of Project BLUE BOOK, the Air Force program for the investigation of UFOS.

The decision to discontinue UFO investigations was based on an evaluation of a report prepared by the University of Colorado entitled, "Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects;" a review of the University of Colorado's report by the National Academy of Sciences; past UFO studies and Air Force experience investigating UFO reports during the 40s, '50s, and '60s.

plain: In 1969 the US Air Force shut down Project Blue Book, its UFO study of the 1950s and 60s, and pointed to a university study as its reason. Robert Salas, a former Air Force officer, tells Michels that when the Air Force wanted to "get out of" the UFO business in 1969, "they even quoted the Condon investigation". He means the Condon report, a study of UFO reports led by Edward Condon, published by the University of Colorado and dated 31 October 1968. Bryce Zabel, a writer on Hollywood and UFOs, tells it without naming Condon: the Air Force, "holding the line", closed Blue Book in '69 and said, in effect, "We're washing our hands of that." The report itself concludes that "further extensive study of UFOs probably cannot be justified in the expectation that science will be advanced thereby". It gives as Condon's "impression" that the defense side could be handled "without the continuance of a special unit such as Project Blue Book", which it calls "a question for defense specialists rather than research scientists". An Air Force fact sheet of January 1985 is the official record: "On December 17, 1969, the Secretary of the Air Force announced the termination of Project BLUE BOOK", a decision it says was based on the Colorado report, a review of it by the National Academy of Sciences, and the Air Force's own experience. Told this way, the story matters because it marks the moment the government publicly stepped away from the subject.
